questions.q: What is the key difference between a functional requirement and a nonfunctional requirement (NFR)?
options: A functional requirement describes what the system does; an NFR describes how well it does it
A functional requirement only applies to Apex code, while an NFR only applies to declarative automation
There is no real difference — the terms are interchangeable in Salesforce architecture
An NFR is always more important to the business than a functional requirement
questions.explain: Functional requirements are testable statements of what a system does (a pass/fail check). NFRs describe quality attributes like speed, availability, and security that shape how well the system performs those functions.

questions.q: Why do NFR gaps typically go unnoticed until production, while functional gaps are caught earlier?
options: NFRs are always documented last in a project plan
Salesforce automatically enforces every NFR during development, so gaps are theoretical
A missing NFR usually only becomes visible under real load, real attack, or real audit scrutiny — conditions a small demo or sales-cycle test never recreates
Functional requirements are tested by QA while NFRs are never tested at all
questions.explain: A functional gap (a button does nothing) is obvious immediately. An NFR gap, like a trigger that's too slow under volume, only surfaces once the system faces conditions a demo with a handful of test records never simulates.

questions.q: Which of the following is this course's six standard NFR categories for Salesforce architecture?
options: Branding, licensing, pricing, procurement, vendor management, contracts
Performance, security, scalability, reliability, maintainability and recoverability, compliance
Apex, SOQL, Flow, Lightning Web Components, Visualforce, APIs
Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Experience Cloud, Marketing Cloud, Commerce Cloud, Data Cloud
questions.explain: The six categories this course organizes NFR work around are performance, security, scalability, reliability, maintainability and recoverability, and compliance.

questions.q: A custom object is designed without considering future data volume, and 18 months later it hits practical limits in production. What does this scenario illustrate about NFRs?
options: That the business analyst, not the architect, is responsible for data-volume decisions
That Salesforce custom objects can never scale, regardless of design
That this is purely a functional requirement problem, unrelated to NFRs
That NFRs decided late, after the fact, turn into a costly migration project instead of a cheap upfront design choice
questions.explain: An NFR like data-volume scalability decided during initial design is a design choice. The same NFR discovered after the fact, once limits are already hit in production, becomes a far more expensive and riskier migration.

questions.q: Which international standard is referenced in this lesson as the common reference point for software quality attribute categories?
options: ISO/IEC 25010
PCI DSS
ISO/IEC 27001
NIST SP 800-53
questions.explain: ISO/IEC 25010 defines the software product quality model that NFR categories like performance, security, and reliability are commonly organized around.
